items.title: Hera’s Didymos asteroid in eclipse
items.snippet: A solar eclipse in deep space, shown in this early view of the Didymos binary asteroids from the European Space Agency’s Hera mission for planetary defence. The smaller Dimorphos moonlet is seen casting its shadow across part of its Didymos parent body, to blank out the Sun across the shaded stretch of rocky surface.

items.title: A black hole the size of an atom could destroy an entire star
items.snippet: MIT scientists have discovered that tiny black holes left over from the Big Bang could slowly devour stars from within, eventually triggering spectacular explosions visible across galaxies. Detecting these unusual cosmic events could reveal the existence of primordial black holes and help solve the mystery of dark matter.

items.title: New EU Bureaucracy Index: EU law has more than doubled since 2010
items.snippet: The new EU Bureaucracy Index measures the volume of EU law in force, and it shows a record high: At the end of 2025, the EU regulations and directives in force comprised around 47,600 standard pages, 118% more than in 2010. items.title: Queensland keeps learning disaster lessons. So why do we keep forgetting them?

items.title: A star's 'obliquity' likely has little impact on a given planet's habitability
items.snippet: A star's axial tilt as it relates to the circumstellar disk that surrounds it is known as stellar obliquity. Over space and time, there are a myriad of solar-type stars with all sorts of obliquities. But the question heretofore has always been what effect a given star's initial obliquity has on the planetary system that forms around it.

items.title: What draws data centers to a community?
items.snippet: As Oklahoma communities weigh new data center development, research co-authored by a University of Oklahoma architecture professor offers insight into what draws major technology companies to locations—and why those choices matter locally.

items.title: Hurricane season wrap-up: El Niño fueled record number of Pacific storms but calmed Atlantic
items.snippet: The 2026 hurricane season, which officially ends on Nov. 30, will be remembered as a year of contrasts between the Atlantic and Pacific, a classic indication of a hurricane season influenced by a very strong El Niño. Below-normal activity across the Atlantic basin was offset by above-average activity in the Pacific, including two disasters in Hawaii.
